title: Looped Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: Weight-shared looped mid-block inside a masked diffusion LM denoiser, trained with stochastic loop count, compared under matched training FLOPs.
one_sentence: Loops two early-middle layers of a 125-170M masked diffusion LM with S~U{1..Smax} in training; at matched total training FLOPs it reaches baseline NLL with 2.3-3.3x fewer FLOPs, beats a deeper 21-layer MDM on GSM8K, and extrapolates loops beyond Smax.
key_contributions: First looped transformer inside a masked diffusion LM denoiser (head / looped mid-block / tail), with uniform random loop count during training and FLOP-matched training by running fewer steps.
Ablations: loop position (early-middle best), number of looped layers (looping more than six layers is worse than baseline at matched FLOPs), and Smax (moderate best).

Mechanistic evidence (Sudoku with forced left-to-right order, mask-to-mask attention growth with S, gains concentrated at intermediate noise levels) and a hidden-state-change stopping rule that cuts average loops from 12 to about 5.

setup.model_sizes: 170M diffusion transformer (12 layers) for LM corpora; 125M, 14-layer Qwen2-style MDM for GSM8K; 1-layer model for Sudoku
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LM1B, OpenWebText, FineWeb-Edu (baseline 1M steps, batch 512); TinyGSM 11.8M problems for GSM8K; 100k Sudoku
setup.loops_train: S ~ U{1..Smax}; Smax=12 (LM), 8 (GSM8K), 6 (Sudoku); looped block = layers 1-2
setup.loops_test: S in {1,6,12,24} (24 beyond Smax); GSM8K S up to 16; adaptive stop with relative hidden-state change < 0.1
setup.baselines: same-size non-looped MDM at matched params and total training FLOPs; 18- and 21-layer MDMs (21-layer matches per-step training FLOPs)
setup.benchmarks: test NLL, generative PPL, zero-shot PPL on 7 corpora, 9 zero-shot downstream tasks, GSM8K, Sudoku

claims.claim: At matched parameters and matched total training FLOPs, LoopMDM reaches the baseline's final test NLL with 3.34x, 2.95x and 2.34x fewer training FLOPs on LM1B, OWT and FineWeb-Edu.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_train_flop (looped model sees fewer tokens)
claims.evidence_quote: For S ≥ 6, LoopMDM consistently outperforms the MDM baseline across all three corpora, reaching the same final NLL with 3.34×, 2.95×, and 2.34× fewer training FLOPs, respectively.

claims.claim: Looping beats a deeper non-looped 21-layer MDM whose per-step training FLOPs match LoopMDM's on GSM8K, so gains are not explained by depth alone (note: at S=8/16 LoopMDM's inference depth exceeds 21 layers).
claims.regime: iso_train_flop vs deeper baseline (deeper baseline has more parameters; not iso-inference-FLOP at S>=8)
claims.evidence_quote: More importantly, it outperforms a 21-layer baseline with comparable per-step FLOPs, achieving gains of +2.7 at S = 8 and +3.4 points at S = 16.

claims.claim: Where to loop matters: looping more than six layers underperforms the non-looped baseline at matched FLOPs; early-middle positions are best.
claims.evidence_quote: In particular, looping more than six layers underperforms the baseline, indicating that simply applying looping to more layers does not lead to more effective use of training FLOPs.

claims.claim: Loop extrapolation: inference with S=24 (> Smax=12) keeps improving NLL; S=1 underperforms the baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: At S = 24, beyond the training maximum Smax = 12, performance continues to improve, indicating that the learned operator generalizes beyond the training regime.

claims.claim: A hidden-state-change stopping rule reduces average loops from 12 to about 5 while preserving most gains.
claims.evidence_quote: adaptive looping reduces the average loop count from S = 12 to roughly five iterations while preserving most of the performance gains across all evaluation settings.

numbers.what: GSM8K gain over same-size 14-layer MDM at S=16, Top-2 / Top-3 unmasking
numbers.quote: At S = 16 (beyond the training maximum Smax = 8), the improvement reaches +8.5 and +8.1 points, respectively.

numbers.what: fraction of training FLOPs to match 14-layer baseline final GSM8K accuracy
numbers.quote: LoopMDM also matches the 14-layer baseline’s final accuracy using only 43% of its training FLOPs.

numbers.what: PTB zero-shot perplexity baseline vs LoopMDM S=12
numbers.quote: achieving gains of 0.3-18.3 points at S = 12, with the largest improvement on PTB (108.5 → 90.2).

numbers.what: Sudoku exact-solve with forced left-to-right order: 1-layer baseline vs looped at S=1
numbers.quote: Meanwhile, the 1-layer MDM baseline achieves only 10.9% accuracy, and the looped model at S = 1 similarly reaches 10.6%

numbers.what: downstream average accuracy, adaptive looping (S 12 -> 4.9 avg)
numbers.quote: Downstream Acc. (↑) 12 → 4.9 41.4 → 41.3

limitations: Looped block and stopping rule are hand-specified; only medium-scale (125-170M) MDMs; billion-scale untested; mechanistic analysis is correlational.
survey_notes: Diffusion-backbone evidence that looping helps even though MDMs already iterate across denoising steps. Strong regime design (iso-param + iso-total-training-FLOP, looped model sees fewer tokens). Agrees with ETD/MoR-style findings that looping a small middle subset beats looping everything; contrast with 2606.18022 (Recursive Scaling in MDMs, sibling group). Deeper-baseline comparison is matched on per-step training FLOPs only; at S=8/16 inference cost exceeds the 21-layer baseline, so it is not iso-inference-FLOP.

title: bioMoR: Biology-Guided Mixture-of-Recursions for Effective Genomic Learning
relevance_reason: Mixture-of-Recursions (shared block, token-level recursion depth routing) applied to gene/pathway tokens with biology-graph-guided routing.
one_sentence: Applies MoR to omics classification with three biology-graph injections (embedding smoothing, attention bias, graph-aware router); with one shared block (75K params, K=4) it beats a 300K-parameter vanilla Transformer, a fixed recursive model and plain MoR on eight datasets.
key_contributions: First MoR backbone for gene- and pathway-token learning, with a shared recursive block and per-token depth up to K.
Biology knowledge (gene co-expression, pathway graphs) injected into embeddings, attention bias and the recursion-depth router.
Controlled architecture ladder (Vanilla, fixed Recursive, MoR expert/token, bioMoR) with FLOP accounting; recursion depths are read out for interpretability.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 8 omics benchmarks (single-cell and pathway-based), five-fold stratified CV; TCGA survival cohorts
setup.loops_train: max depth K=4 in main table; K=2,3,4 in efficiency study
setup.baselines: Vanilla Transformer, fixed-depth Recursive Transformer, MoR (expert/token choice), external scBiGNN, TabNet, Pathformer, scGPT-style etc.
setup.benchmarks: macro-F1 and balanced accuracy on Segerstolpe, Lung, T-cell, Muraro, Spleen, BLCA, PAN-2M, PAN-3M; survival risk

claims.claim: With effective depth aligned to the vanilla Transformer (K=4), bioMoR improves average macro-F1 by 8.2 points and balanced accuracy by 7.1 points over the best non-bioMoR baseline with 75% fewer parameters.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth + iso_data (same folds); gains attributed to biology priors, plain recursion alone is slightly below vanilla
claims.evidence_quote: To align effective depth with the base Transformer, denoted Vanilla, all recursive models in Table 1 use K=4. Both bioMoR routing variants outperform these baselines on average for both metrics.

claims.claim: bioMoR keeps about 69-70% macro-F1 across recursion depths K=2..4 with fewer FLOPs than vanilla; at K=2 it uses 58% fewer FLOPs.
claims.regime: unclear (FLOP comparison vs vanilla at varying K)
claims.evidence_quote: bioMoR consistently maintains approximately 69– 70% macro-F1 across all recursion depths while requiring fewer FLOPs than Vanilla. At K=2, bioMoR uses 58% fewer FLOPs than Vanilla.

numbers.what: Average macro-F1: Vanilla (300K) vs fixed Recursive (75K) vs bioMoR-Expert (75K)
fixed-depth Recursive row macro-F1 (avg 64.6)
bioMoR-Expert macro-F1 row (avg 74.6)
external comparison PAN-2M macro-F1
numbers.quote: bioMoR obtains the highest mean macro-F1 in both panels: 0.86±0.01 on PAN-2M, compared with 0.84±0.01 for scBiGNN

limitations: Very small models (75K parameters); gains come mainly from biology priors rather than recursion; limitations not explicitly discussed.
survey_notes: Science/genomics transfer of MoR. Key nuance for survey: in Table 1 the plain fixed-depth Recursive model (75K) is slightly below the 300K vanilla (64.6 vs 65.9 avg macro-F1), and biology-agnostic MoR is about equal (66.1/66.4); the 8.2-point gain comes from domain-informed routing/attention, so looping per se buys parameter efficiency (4x fewer params at near parity), not accuracy. Paper carries an AAAI copyright line but no explicit acceptance statement.

title: The Thinking Pixel: Recursive Sparse Reasoning in Multimodal Diffusion Latents
relevance_reason: Recursion is a short (2-5 step) loop over the joint-attention component of selected DiT/SD3 layers with per-step LoRA adapters chosen by a gate; component-level, finetuned on pretrained weights.
one_sentence: Inserts a recursive sparse mixture-of-adapters module into the joint attention of DiT-XL and SD3-medium layers, iterating visual tokens over a few latent steps with gated per-step LoRA experts; reports small FID and GenEval gains over the base models and an SFT baseline.
key_contributions: Recursive sparse joint-attention component with Gumbel-Softmax gating over M LoRA modules, conditioned on vision tokens, diffusion timestep and condition.
Recursive adapter updates accumulate module outputs across T_latent steps on top of a frozen base layer.
Evaluation on ImageNet 256 class-conditional (DiT-XL), GenEval/DPG text-to-image (SD3-medium) and FrozenLake navigation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet; 1000 MSCOCO samples for T2I finetuning
setup.loops_train: T_latent in {2,5} latent steps with M in {2,5} modules
setup.baselines: DiT-XL/2, SD3-medium, SD3-medium + LoRA SFT, ADM, LDM, U-ViT, DiffuSSM

claims.claim: On GenEval, recursion with modulation over multiple SD3 layers gives the best overall score (71.18) vs SD3-medium (67.93) and same-data LoRA SFT (69.55); both recursion and modulation contribute.
claims.regime: iso_data vs SFT (same finetuning data); FLOPs not matched
claims.evidence_quote: The results show that both recursion and modulation contribute to the improvement of model performance. Targeting multiple layers of SD3 further enhances its benefits and achieves the best overall scores on the benchmark.

claims.claim: On ImageNet 256 the method is competitive with DiT-XL/2 at the same reported size (FID 2.27 vs 2.34).
claims.evidence_quote: framework achieves competitive performance with the baseline DiT-XL/2 model. DiffuSSM-XL achieved better sFID and precision scores.

numbers.what: GenEval overall SD3-medium
GenEval overall, multiple layers: SFT vs Ours (M=2, T=2)

limitations: May not find the optimal latent computation depth for longer recursions; loop counts are tiny (2-5) and gains are small.
builds_on: Geiping et al. test-time latent reasoning
survey_notes: Diffusion-backbone example where looping is applied to a single sub-component with per-step LoRA (relaxed sharing), retrofitted onto a pretrained generator. Evidence is weak: compute is not matched, gains are 1-2 GenEval points over SFT, and the 'w/o recursion' ablation (69.88) is close to the full model at the middle layer (70.66).

title: LoopICL: Looping a single transformer block to solve tabular tasks
relevance_reason: Tabular foundation model made of a single weight-shared two-stream block looped L times, with random loop counts in pretraining, residual scaling, and a learned exit gate.
one_sentence: A ~3.25M-parameter tabular ICL model loops one cell/row-stream block (L ~ 1+Poisson(LogNormal), clipped to 8, in pretraining); at 12 loops it is competitive with TabICLv2 at similar dominant FLOPs with 88.2% fewer parameters, and extrapolates to about twice its pretraining loop budget.
key_contributions: Single looped two-stream transformer block for tabular in-context learning, with distributional input conditioning that stabilizes recurrent training.
Residual scaling study: alpha=1 is best within trained loop range but degrades beyond; alpha=1/L-type scaling extrapolates past the pretraining limit.
Learned early-exit gate trained on frozen backbone (up to 16 loops) giving per-dataset compute adaptation on TabArena and TALENT.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic prior tasks (Stage 1 100K steps; Stage 2 30K steps up to 100,000 rows with TBPTT window 5)
setup.loops_train: L ~ 1 + Poisson(gamma), gamma ~ LogNormal, clipped to [1,8], mean 5.32
setup.loops_test: fixed L up to 20, best around 12; early-exit gate trained up to 16
setup.baselines: 6 stacked blocks (fixed-depth TFM) at matched pretraining; TabICLv2, TabPFN family and other TFMs/GBDTs on TabArena and TALENT
setup.benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT classification (Elo, improvability), 54-dataset development set, synthetic prior tasks

claims.claim: Versus 6 stacked blocks matching the mean pretraining loop count, the looped model has higher in-distribution loss on synthetic priors but lower loss on real development tasks (better generalization).
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, the recurrent variants achieve lower loss on the development set tasks, indicating better generalization to unseen tasks.

claims.claim: Recurrence makes optimization harder (larger gradient norms); distributional conditioning stabilizes it.
claims.evidence_quote: we observe that recurrent models are more challenging to train, exhibiting generally larger gradient norms.

claims.claim: At 12 loops LoopICL is competitive with TabICLv2 whose 12 blocks give the same dominant FLOPs, with 88.2% fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: TabICLv2 uses 12 ICL blocks and hidden dimensions of the same size as LoopICL, thus, the dominant FLOPs cost is the same

claims.claim: Loop extrapolation depends on residual scaling: alpha=1 degrades at high loop counts, while 1/L-type scaling extrapolates beyond the pretraining limit; the deployed model works at about twice the mean training loops.
claims.evidence_quote: these results demonstrate that our model robustly extrapolates beyond its pretraining limit on real-world tasks and operates effectively at roughly twice the average number of loop steps observed during pretraining.

numbers.what: parameter reduction vs TabICLv2
numbers.quote: Notably, LoopICL achieves this at 88.2% fewer parameters.

numbers.what: model size
numbers.quote: In total, the model has ∼3.25M parameters with ∼2.7M parameters in the recurrent block.

numbers.what: mean loops during pretraining after clipping
numbers.quote: We choose µ such that E[L] = 6 before clipping, meaning the model learns on average from 5.32 loops during pretraining

numbers.what: early-exit at lambda=90 vs 12 fixed loops on TabArena
numbers.quote: On TabArena, EE is faster on 33 out of 38 datasets, and 12 out of 38 datasets gain both speed and accuracy simultaneously.

limitations: Classification only; single-block model at small scale; scaling laws and repeating N layers left to future work.
builds_on: Geiping et al. 2502.05171 (log-normal Poisson loop sampling)
survey_notes: Tabular domain is a clean case where looping buys parameter efficiency without accuracy loss because the task is algorithmic (iterative refinement of class separability) rather than knowledge-heavy; authors explicitly contrast with knowledge-intensive LMs. Reproduces language-side recipes (Huginn loop sampler, TBPTT). The residual-scaling-vs-extrapolation finding parallels language results that normalization/scaling controls loop extrapolation; contrast DéjàView 2605.30215 which does not extrapolate. The TabICLv2 comparison is approximately iso-inference-FLOP but unmatched in training.

title: Thinking in Depth, Speaking Directly: Recurrent Latent Reasoning for Paralinguistically Grounded Spoken Dialogue
relevance_reason: Retrofits a weight-shared 3-layer loop (L9-11, 4 passes) into the Qwen2.5-Omni-7B speech LM decoder, with per-pass acoustic memory re-anchoring.
one_sentence: LoopSLM loops decoder layers 9-11 of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B four times, re-injecting a multi-depth acoustic memory each pass; CoT-supervised loop training then a direct-response coda gives better paralinguistic reasoning than CoT-SFT with 64.5% fewer tokens.
key_contributions: First looped-transformer speech LM: Prelude (L1-8, frozen) / Loop (L9-11 shared, R=4) / Transition / Coda, executed depth 28 -> 37 layer calls.
ReCue: per-pass cross-attention to a compact multi-scale audio-encoder memory with iteration embedding and zero-init gates.

Two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 trains only the Loop+ReCue on speech-grounded CoT; Stage 2 trains only the Coda on direct responses; block-replacement control shows gains come from the learned recurrent transform, not depth.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 380,540 utterances (431.9 h) bilingual dialogue with Gemini-annotated Cue/Need/Risk/Plan traces
setup.loops_train: R=4 (ablations R=1,2,3,6)
setup.baselines: Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and other off-the-shelf SLMs; CoT-SFT on same data and base; Qwen3-Omni-Thinking (30B MoE)
setup.benchmarks: EchoMind (understanding, reasoning, reply C1-C4), SD-Eval, MMSU, MMAU-Pro

claims.claim: Against CoT-SFT on the same base and data, LoopSLM gains over 20 points in reasoning accuracy with 64.5% fewer generated tokens.
claims.regime: iso_param + iso_data (looped uses more depth per token, fewer tokens)
claims.evidence_quote: Relative to the matched Qwen2.5 CoT-SFT baseline, it gains over 20 percentage points in reasoning accuracy with 64.5% fewer generated tokens.

claims.claim: At fixed executed depth, replacing passes with stock (untrained) blocks gives little benefit, while trained recurrent passes give progressively larger gains, so the benefit comes from the learned recurrent transform rather than extra layer evaluations.
claims.evidence_quote: These results show that the benefit comes from the learned recurrent transformation rather than additional layer evaluations alone.

claims.claim: More trained loops are not monotonically better: R=4 best; R=6 hurts reasoning and format adherence.
claims.evidence_quote: Models trained at different recurrence depths show that the benefit is not monotonic (Table 2, bottom). R4 gives the strongest overall reasoning.

claims.claim: Loop placement matters: looping L9-11 beats L15-17 on understanding and reasoning; L3-5 harms transcription.
claims.evidence_quote: Looping L9–11 rather than L15–17 improves understanding and reasoning on EchoMind by 6.29 and 3.57 points, respectively, whereas L15–17 improves response style.

numbers.what: executed depth with 4 passes
numbers.quote: At inference, the four passes run during prompt processing and at each decoding step, increasing executed depth from 28 to 37 layer calls without duplicating Transformer weights.

numbers.what: gain over Qwen2.5-Omni-7B in understanding / reasoning accuracy
numbers.quote: LoopSLM improves mean paralinguistic understanding and reasoning accuracy on EchoMind by 9.8 and 6.6 points, respectively

numbers.what: latency vs Qwen3-Omni-Thinking
numbers.quote: It also outperforms Qwen3-Omni-Thinking [11] on most metrics of empathetic reply quality with 34× lower latency.

numbers.what: R=6 understanding accuracy (S/H)

limitations: Fixed R=4 trained loop count; deeper loops degrade format adherence; relies on LLM-annotated CoT traces and LLM judges.
survey_notes: Speech-LM retrofit; replaces explicit CoT tokens with recurrent depth (sequence axis -> depth axis), a key 'looping vs CoT' data point outside text. Block-replacement control is a useful methodological template for separating 'more layer calls' from 'learned recurrence'. Placement finding (early-middle loop best for reasoning) agrees with LoopMDM 2605.26106 and ETD. Comparisons with off-the-shelf SLMs are unmatched.

title: Parameter Efficient Multimodal Transformers for Video Representation Learning
relevance_reason: ALBERT-style cross-layer weight sharing (plus low-rank cross-modality sharing) in audio-visual Transformers to cut memory; looping used only as a parameter-saving device, no loop-count study.
one_sentence: Shares Transformer weights across layers (ALBERT-style) and, via a low-rank U shared with private Sigma*V^T, across visual/audio/multimodal Transformers, reducing Transformer parameters from 128M to 4M so audio-visual models can be pretrained end-to-end on 30-second Kinetics-700 clips.
key_contributions: Decomposes each Transformer weight into a shared low-rank factor (shared across modality Transformers) and private parts, combined with cross-layer sharing.
Up to 97% parameter reduction enabling end-to-end training of CNN + multimodal Transformer from scratch.
Content-aware negative sampling for the masked embedding prediction objective.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Kinetics-700 (410K videos, 30 s clips) or AudioSet (1.8M clips); 64 V100, 220K iterations
setup.loops_train: 6 layers per Transformer with cross-layer sharing (Vis-2 / Vis-6 ablations)
setup.baselines: no sharing, cross-layer only, all-sharing; prior audio-visual methods
setup.benchmarks: Kinetics-Sounds, other audio-visual and unimodal classification downstream tasks

claims.claim: Cross-layer weight sharing does not hurt audio-visual classification performance (same depth, same data), confirming ALBERT's finding in the multimodal setting.
claims.evidence_quote: The results show that sharing weights across layers does not hurt the performance, confirming the observations by Lan et al. (2020) in the audio-visual setting.

claims.claim: The combined sharing scheme reduces Transformer parameters by 97%.
claims.evidence_quote: Our parameter reduction scheme reduces the number of parameters from 128M to 4M (by 97%) (Table 1 (c)).

limitations: Sharing is motivated by memory, not compute scaling; no study of loop count or inference-time depth.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2021
survey_notes: Early multimodal instance of the 'sharing for memory/parameter efficiency' motivation; looping per se is not studied, and the shared stack is fixed depth. Use as lineage evidence that ALBERT-style sharing transfers to audio-visual video Transformers at iso-depth.

title: LoopVLA: Learning Sufficiency in Recurrent Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Models
relevance_reason: Retrofits a VLA (Qwen3VL-2B backbone) into frozen perceptual layers plus a weight-shared looped block with per-iteration action and learned sufficiency (halting) heads.
one_sentence: Keeps the first 4 Qwen3VL-2B decoder layers frozen, loops 3 retained layers up to 8 times (matching the 24 replaced layers), predicts an action and a sufficiency score each iteration, and halves VLA parameters while matching or beating the full-depth policy on LIBERO.
key_contributions: Recurrent VLA: perceptual anchor layers + shared Loop Block (L x N, default 3x8) with action head and sufficiency head at every iteration.
Self-supervised distribution-alignment objective: per-iteration confidence distribution trained to match the normalized negative action-loss profile, giving learned halting without labels.
Fixed-budget ablation of L x N = 24 shows balanced depth/iteration splits beat extremes; adaptive exit beats any fixed exit layer.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: LIBERO suites (joint training), VLA-Arena-L0-Small; LIBERO-Plus zero-shot
setup.loops_train: fixed N iterations (default 3 layers x 8 loops), all iterations supervised
setup.loops_test: optimal selection over N, trade-off alpha, fixed loops, or halting distribution
setup.baselines: Qwen3OFT / Qwen3FM (same backbone, full depth), pi0, pi0.5, OpenVLA, GR00T-N1.5, UniVLA, etc.

claims.claim: With the same backbone and training, LoopOFT* (1.2B, all 8 loops) reaches 96.0% average LIBERO success vs 94.9% for the 2.2B full-depth Qwen3OFT at the same 0.53T FLOPs.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop + iso_effective_depth + iso_data (looped has ~45% fewer params)
claims.evidence_quote: LoopOFT* attains an average success rate of 96.0%, outperforming strong baselines such as π0 and Qwen3OFT, despite using fewer parameters.

claims.claim: At a fixed L x N = 24 budget, balanced splits (4x6, 3x8) are best; neither more unique depth nor more iterations alone is sufficient.
claims.evidence_quote: This suggests that neither increasing depth nor iteration alone is sufficient; instead, effective performance arises from a proper balance between the two.

claims.claim: Adaptive (sufficiency-based) exit selection beats any fixed exit iteration, and optimal depth varies by task suite.
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, adaptive selection (∗) consistently outperforms fixed strategies, indicating that the optimal computation depth is input-dependent.

numbers.what: LIBERO rows (Long / Avg / Params / FLOPs / Hz) for Qwen3OFT, LoopOFT0, LoopOFTalpha, LoopOFT*
numbers.value: Qwen3OFT 94.9 avg 2.2B 0.53T 10.49 Hz; LoopOFT* 96.0 avg 1.2B 0.53T 10.93 Hz; LoopOFT0 94.6 avg 0.31T 18.41 Hz

numbers.what: parameter reduction and throughput gain (abstract)
numbers.quote: reducing parameters by 45% and improving inference throughput by up to 1.7 times while matching or outperforming strong baselines in task success.

limitations: Reduced capacity hurts on hardest LIBERO-Plus factors (robot variation); simulation-only evaluation.
survey_notes: Robotics retrofit with learned halting; strong same-backbone iso-inference-FLOP comparison (LoopOFT* vs Qwen3OFT at 0.53T). The non-monotonic L x N trade-off under fixed effective depth mirrors LoopVLA-style findings in language (MoR, ETD). Per-iteration supervision of all loops is deep supervision; halting is learned from loss profile (similar in spirit to Ouro's entropy-regularized exit). External baseline comparisons (pi0, OpenVLA) are unmatched.

title: ELT: Elastic Looped Transformers for Visual Generation
relevance_reason: Weight-shared N-layer block looped L times inside masked-generative and diffusion image/video generators, trained with intra-loop self-distillation for any-time inference.
one_sentence: ELT loops an N-layer block L times per generation step in MaskGIT/MAGVIT/DiT backbones and trains a random early-exit student against the full-loop teacher (ILSD); at iso-inference-compute it matches MaskGIT-XL FID 2.0 with 4x fewer parameters and supports any-time loop counts.
key_contributions: N x L looped visual generators (masked generative and diffusion) with effective depth N*L at N unique layers.

Intra-Loop Self Distillation with stochastic student sampling: student exits at L_int ~ U(L_min, L_max) and is distilled from the stop-grad full-loop teacher, at no extra training forward cost; vanilla looping only works at L = L_max.
Iso-inference-compute scaling study (FID vs GFLOPs, params) and TPU throughput gains (up to 3.5x) from on-chip parameter reuse.

setup.model_sizes: 69M-1.1B ELT (DiT variants); widths d=1024-1536; 76M for video
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet 256x256; UCF-101 (~13.7M training tokens)
setup.loops_train: fixed L_max with stochastic student exit (e.g., 8N x 4L, 16N x 2L, 4N x 8L)
setup.baselines: MaskGIT-XL, MAGVIT, DiT 16- and 32-layer (1.1B, 2.1B), vanilla looped transformers without ILSD
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet 256 FID/IS, UCF-101 FVD, throughput on TPU v6e

claims.claim: In DiT, looped 16N x 2L (1.1B) and 8N x 4L (539M) beat the 32-layer 2.1B DiT at the same inference compute; the 1.1B looped model also beats the same-size 16-layer DiT (2.83 vs 3.87).
claims.evidence_quote: ELT outperforms the baseline model with 32 layers (FID 3.43) using iso-inference-compute 8 𝑁 × 4 𝐿 (FID 3.16) and 16 𝑁 × 2 𝐿 (FID 2.83) settings, achieving 4× and 2× reduction in parameter count respectively.

claims.claim: A single unique layer looped 32 times fails (FID 10.30): a minimum block size N is needed.
claims.evidence_quote: The 1 𝑁 × 32 𝐿 configuration (FID 10.30) reveals that a single unique transformer layer, despite 32 effective passes, lacks the representational capacity for high-fidelity generation

claims.claim: Vanilla looping only gives coherent images at the training loop count; ILSD enables any-time inference across loop counts.
claims.evidence_quote: standard looping only produces a coherent image when the inference loop count exactly matches its training setup ( 𝐿 = 8), with quality severely degrading at all other values.

claims.claim: Increasing loops at fixed N keeps improving FID with diminishing returns; beyond a point, moving to a larger model beats over-looping a small one.
claims.evidence_quote: the gains eventually diminish, where transitioning to the next architecture scale becomes more performant than over-looping smaller models.

claims.claim: In data-constrained video generation, a 76M looped model beats MAGVIT at iso-inference-compute, which the authors read as robustness to overfitting.
claims.evidence_quote: Our compact 76M ELT model outperforms MAGVIT baseline (FVD 72.8 vs 76) on data-constrained settings of UCF-101 (∼13.7M training tokens) in iso-inference-compute settings.

numbers.what: ImageNet 256 FID of ELT-XL vs MaskGIT-XL
numbers.quote: Despite using 4× less parameters, ELT-XL achieves same FID of 2.0 as MaskGIT-XL, which is the base setup for ELT.

numbers.what: DiT 16-layer / 32-layer FID and params
numbers.quote: DiT - 16 layers DiT - 32 layers 3.87 3.43 1.1B 2.1B 16 32

numbers.what: peak TPU throughput speedup
numbers.quote: ELT achieves a peak speedup of 3.5× for model scale H.

numbers.what: UCF-101 FVD with more loops and sampling steps
numbers.quote: Scaling the compute further with number of loops and sampling steps gives a boost in performance, reaching FVD of 60.8.

limitations: Very small blocks (N=1) fail; over-looping small models is dominated by larger models at equal GFLOPs; explicit limitations section not found.
survey_notes: Key generation-domain result with clean iso-inference-FLOP and iso-param comparisons: at 1.1B, 16N x 2L beats both iso-param DiT-16 and iso-FLOP DiT-32. Diminishing returns of loops at fixed N agree with language scaling results (looped models gain from depth but parameters still matter). ILSD (random early-exit student distilled from full-loop teacher) is the vision analogue of loop-count randomization; without it, vanilla looped generators collapse off the training loop count, agreeing with DéjàView 2605.30215's lack of extrapolation and contrasting with LoopMDM's randomized training that extrapolates. Throughput gains come from memory-wall arithmetic intensity, a systems argument also made in language.

key: t:mor swin efficient vision transformer using mixture of recursions
title: MoR–Swin: Efficient Vision Transformer Using Mixture of Recursions
relevance_reason: Integrates Mixture-of-Recursions token-level adaptive recursion (shared blocks + router) into Swin Transformer.
one_sentence: Adds MoR-style recursive window attention and a load-balanced token router to Swin; on ImageNet, COCO and ADE20K it reports about 50% fewer parameters and up to 2x faster inference within about 0.5 points of Swin-B (abstract only).
key_contributions: Recursive window attention module for Swin.
Lightweight token router with load balancing loss assigning per-token recursion depth.
Evaluation on classification, detection and segmentation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K; COCO; ADE20K
setup.baselines: Swin-B

claims.claim: MoR-Swin halves parameters and speeds inference up to 2x at a modest accuracy cost relative to Swin-B.
claims.evidence_quote: MoR–Swin reduces parameters by about 50% and accelerates inference up to twofold at a modest accuracy cost (within about 0.5 points of Swin-B on ImageNet-1K).

survey_notes: Non-arXiv letter; abstract only (fulltext unavailable). MoR transfers to hierarchical vision backbones as a parameter/latency saver with small accuracy loss; no evidence of accuracy gains. Compare Soft MoR ViT 2607.00774 and MoR-ST (both in sibling or this list).

title: LoopViT: Scaling Visual ARC with Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Weight-tied hybrid conv+attention ViT core iterated T times for pixel-level ARC reasoning, with entropy-based dynamic exit.
one_sentence: Loop-ViT iterates a weight-tied Hybrid Block (depthwise conv + attention, with step embeddings) for a fixed T in training and halts by predictive entropy at test time; the 18M model reaches 65.8% on ARC-AGI-1 vs 54.5% for the same-size feed-forward VARC ViT.
key_contributions: Looped vision transformer for ARC from pixels: weight-tied Hybrid Block (DW-Conv + MHSA) with learned step embeddings and identity extrapolation beyond the training step count.
Parameter-free Dynamic Exit based on predictive entropy; fixed-depth training (e.g., T=12) with final-output supervision.
Space-time ablation (core depth B vs iterations T): small cores gain most from more iterations; Hybrid core beats vanilla at all depths.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ARC + RE-ARC, offline pretraining then test-time training on demonstrations
setup.loops_train: fixed T (e.g., T=12), supervision on final output
setup.loops_test: dynamic exit by entropy up to Tmax (e.g., T in [4,8] in ablation)
setup.baselines: VARC 18M and 73M ensemble ViTs; HRM 27M, TRM 7M; LLMs

claims.claim: At equal parameters (18M), the looped ViT beats the feed-forward VARC ViT on ARC-AGI-1 (65.8 vs 54.5) and the 73M VARC ensemble (60.4); compute is higher due to unrolling.
claims.regime: iso_param (vs VARC 18M); FLOPs not matched; ensemble comparison unmatched
claims.evidence_quote: By recycling weights across iterations, Loop-ViT (Large) achieves 65.8% on ARC-1, surpassing the 73M VARC ensemble.

claims.claim: A 3.8M Loop-ViT beats the 18M VARC baseline with about one fifth of the parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: a 3.8M parameter Loop-ViT (Small) reaches 60.1% score on ARC-1, surpassing the 18M VARC baseline (54.5%) with roughly one-fifth of the parameters

claims.claim: Entropy-based dynamic exit (T in [4,8]) gives higher accuracy at lower average compute than a fixed 6-step model.
claims.evidence_quote: the Dynamic Exit mechanism achieves higher accuracy while using lower average inference compute on ARC-AGI-1.

claims.claim: Low-capacity cores benefit most from added iterations; high-capacity cores keep scaling with T up to the limit.
claims.regime: iso_param per core depth, varying compute
claims.evidence_quote: For low-capacity cores (B = 2), increasing T yields the most significant gains as weight-tied recurrence emulates the expressive depth of larger models

numbers.what: ARC-AGI-1 / ARC-AGI-2 for VARC 18M, VARC ensemble 73M, Loop-ViT S/M/L
numbers.quote: 18M 54.5 73M 60.4 8.3 11.1 Loop-ViT (Small) Loop-ViT (Medium) Loop-ViT (Large) 3.8M 11.2M 18M 60.1 63.8 65.8 10.0 11.5 14.2

numbers.what: accuracy of samples exiting at step 5
numbers.quote: samples that exit early (e.g., at Step 5) yield high accuracy (83.33%), whereas those requiring more iterations (Step 8)

limitations: Fixed-depth training only; relies on test-time training; ARC-AGI-2 accuracy remains low (14.2%).
survey_notes: Vision-reasoning analogue of HRM/TRM: looping a ViT on ARC grids beats the same-parameter feed-forward ViT, but compute is not matched (iso-param only). Inductive bias (local conv) matters inside the loop, a design choice with no language counterpart. Entropy-based halting parallels language confidence-based exits. Cited by ELT 2604.09168 as prior looped-ViT work.

title: On the Role of Computation in Reinforcement Learning
relevance_reason: Theory plus experiments on weight-shared recurrent-depth (iterated gated MLP block, input injected each step) policies/value nets in RL, separating compute from parameters.
one_sentence: Formalizes compute-bounded RL policies, proves more compute can solve and horizon-generalize where less cannot, and shows a minimal recurrent block (IRU) applied N times improves performance and long-horizon generalization over parameter-matched MLPs and larger ResNets on 31 RL tasks.
key_contributions: Theory: policies as bounded models of computation; MDPs exist where more compute time is arbitrarily better and where low-compute policies overfit while high-compute ones generalize to longer horizons.
Minimal interpolation recurrent unit (IRU) applied N times between an input layer and output head, usable with DQN, IQL, PPO, CRL.

Experiments on 31 online/offline tasks: more recurrent steps help (up to 10x on boxpick/OGBench manipulation); horizon generalization to unseen far goals; recurrent ResNet blocks do not get the same benefit.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: online (boxpick, lightsout) and offline (OGBench) RL; 5 seeds
setup.loops_train: fixed N in {1,2,5,10}
setup.loops_test: same N; 'value of compute' estimated by temporarily changing steps
setup.baselines: MLP (similar params), ResNet (same effective depth, ~5x params), LSTM, recurrent ResNet, TRM-style deep recursion
setup.benchmarks: boxpick, lightsout, OGBench goal-reaching tasks, longer-horizon test tasks

claims.claim: More recurrent steps substantially improve RL performance, up to about 10x on hard boxpick and OGBench manipulation tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: In the challenging boxpick tasks, or the manipulation tasks in ogbench, performance increases up to 10 times after increasing the recurrent steps from one to ten.

claims.claim: IRU-(10) beats a ResNet baseline that uses about 2x more compute and 5x more parameters, and beats the parameter-matched MLP on all tasks.
claims.regime: iso_param (vs MLP); vs ResNet the paper describes it both as same effective depth and as ~2x compute
claims.evidence_quote: This is despite the ResNet using ≈ 2× more compute and ≈ 5× more parameters than IRU-(10).

claims.claim: Recurrent policies trained on nearby goals generalize better to unseen longer-horizon tasks (beat MLP on all, ResNet on 4/6), with more stable training.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 4 shows that IRU outperforms MLP on all tasks and ResNet on 4/6 tasks, and the IRU is more sample efficient on all tasks.

claims.claim: Gating is needed: recurrent ResNet blocks do not get the compute benefit, and TRM-style deep recursion works worse.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that the recurrent ResNet blocks do not achieve the same benefits of added compute.

numbers.what: parameter counts in boxpick
numbers.quote: For instance, in the boxpick tasks the IRU contains 500K parameters, while the ResNet contains 3M parameters.

limitations: Fixed number of recurrent steps for all states (no adaptive compute); no transformer-based recurrence; theory uses single-tape Turing machines and time complexity only.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
builds_on: Schwarzschild et al. 2021 / Bansal et al. 2022 (DeepThinking)
survey_notes: Theory + RL evidence that compute (recurrent depth) and parameters are separate axes for policies; horizon generalization is the RL analogue of length/difficulty extrapolation in DeepThinking and looped LMs. Note an internal inconsistency in the ResNet baseline description (Sec. 6.2 says similar compute/same effective depth; Sec. 6.1 says ResNet uses ~2x more compute). Finding that recurrent ResNet blocks do not benefit and gating is necessary contrasts with language looped transformers that use plain residual blocks; TRM-style deep recursion underperforms here, a contradiction with TRM's success on puzzles.

title: LoopVAE: Recurrent Depth Across Scales for Visual Tokenization
relevance_reason: Visual tokenizer (VAE) whose 4-block core is tied across loop steps and spatial scales (28 block applications per branch), with scale/loop embeddings and gated input injection.
one_sentence: LoopVAE reuses one scale- and loop-conditioned 4-block core across all resolutions of a VAE tokenizer (schedule [1,2,4]); a 29M CNN reaches 0.28 rFID on ImageNet-256 with ~65% fewer parameters than 84M VAEs, but costs 1.57x MACs and 2.85x latency.
key_contributions: Recurrent depth across spatial scales: shared fixed-resolution core with scale + loop embeddings and gated input injection; resolution transitions stay unshared.
Controlled Transformer ablation at fixed execution graph (28 block applications): global sharing (4 stored blocks) has best PSNR/SSIM, fully unshared (28) best LPIPS.

Loop interventions (truncation, bypass) and runtime profiling: trained passes matter even when updates are small; truncation is not a reliable early exit; parameter savings do not reduce compute or latency.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-256, ~30 epochs (15 without GAN + 15 with GAN)
setup.loops_train: fixed schedule [1,2,4] passes per scale over a 4-block core (28 block applications per branch)
setup.baselines: 84M reference VAEs incl. FLUX-VAE (unmatched recipes); scale-wise shared and fully unshared variants (ablation)
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-256 rFID, PSNR, LPIPS, SSIM; TokBench case analysis; downstream diffusion FID

claims.claim: At a fixed execution graph, global sharing (one seventh the stored core blocks) beats fully unshared processing on PSNR and SSIM, while unshared wins on LPIPS.
claims.evidence_quote: Global sharing has the highest PSNR and SSIM, exceeding fully unshared processing by 0.120 dB and 0.0023, respectively, while using one seventh as many stored core blocks.

claims.claim: The 29M looped CNN tokenizer is competitive with 84M VAEs but baselines use unmatched recipes, so no causal advantage of recurrence is claimed.
claims.evidence_quote: Training recipes are not controlled, so quality differences cannot be attributed solely to recurrence or operator choice.

claims.claim: Weight reuse does not reduce execution cost: the looped CNN uses more MACs and higher latency than a Flux-style reference.
claims.evidence_quote: Runtime profiling shows that the 8x looped CNN stores 65.3% fewer parameters than a local Flux-style reference, but uses 1.57× its estimated MACs and 2.85× its batch latency.

claims.claim: Small feature updates in a trained pass still matter a lot (bypass loses ~7.8 dB), and truncation produces output-range errors, so the recurrence is not an any-time decoder.
claims.evidence_quote: feature by only 7.47–9.36% across images, yet bypassing it loses 4.00–11.94 dB PSNR (mean 7.78 dB).

numbers.what: LoopVAE-CNN ImageNet-256 reconstruction
numbers.quote: the 29M-parameter LoopVAE-CNN reaches 0.28 rFID, 32.54 PSNR, 0.048 LPIPS, and 0.91 SSIM (Table 1).

limitations: Single-run sharing ablation; unmatched baseline recipes; no test-time depth extrapolation or compute-matched advantage; no early exit; higher MACs and latency than unshared reference.
survey_notes: Unusually careful about evidence boundaries: explicitly states no compute-matched advantage and no extrapolation. Useful counterweight to throughput claims (ELT 2604.09168 reports TPU speedups from parameter reuse; LoopVAE measures 2.85x higher latency on its CNN tokenizer, since high-resolution compute dominates). Truncation results agree with ELT/DéjàView that intermediate loop states are not usable without explicit training for it. New design axis: sharing across spatial scales, not just depth.

title: Investigating Single-Block Recurrence in Vision Transformers for Image Recognition
relevance_reason: Replaces the whole ViT stack with one shared block applied 12 times, compared against ViTs at matched recipe and compute.
one_sentence: A single shared ViT block applied 12 times nearly matches ViT-B/L on ImageNet-1K at the same compute (0.779 vs 0.789; 0.805 vs 0.808) with 10-20x fewer parameters, but fails at narrow width (ViT-S: 0.681 vs 0.782); extra recurrence does not fix it, width does.
key_contributions: Full-sharing limit of ViT depth trained from scratch with matched recipes and compute for S/B/L widths.

Width is the key factor: narrow single-block models lose ~10 points; increasing recurrence from 12 to 18 steps or heads does not help, while widening does; at fixed parameters, width beats unique depth.
Mechanistic analyses of shared heads/neurons across steps (step-conditioned spectral pruning) and a single LoRA shared across all recurrent steps for parameter-efficient transfer.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K, same recipe as ViT baselines
setup.loops_train: 12 steps (ablation up to 18)
setup.baselines: ViT-S/B/L with identical recipe and compute; hybrid kB x mS allocations; parameter-matched narrow ViTs
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-1K top-1; downstream transfer (Aircraft, EuroSAT, etc.) with linear probe, full FT, LoRA

claims.claim: At sufficient width, a single block reused 12 times nearly matches ViT-B and ViT-L at the same training recipe and compute with ~10-20x fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: The correspondence is even closer for the large model, with bViT-L reaching 0.805 compared with 0.808 for ViT-L, while reducing the parameter count from 304.3M to 14.6M.

claims.claim: At narrow width (384), full sharing loses ~10 points and more recurrent steps or heads do not close the gap.
claims.evidence_quote: At an embedding dimension of 384, bViT-S reaches only 0.681 accuracy compared with 0.782 for ViT-S.

claims.claim: At fixed 12 block evaluations and width, accuracy rises monotonically as more computation is assigned to unique blocks.
claims.evidence_quote: Accuracy improves progressively as more of the computation is assigned to distinct blocks, from 0.681 with one block repeated 12 times to 0.782 with 12 independently parameterized blocks.

claims.claim: At a fixed ~8.7M parameter budget, a wide single-block model beats narrower multi-block ViTs (not FLOP matched).
claims.evidence_quote: As capacity is shifted from representation width toward independently parameterized blocks, accuracy decreases monotonically from 0.779 for bViTB to 0.747 for a 12-block ViT with embedding dimension 240

numbers.what: ImageNet-1K bViT-B vs ViT-B accuracy and params
numbers.quote: bViT-B achieves 0.779 validation accuracy compared with 0.789 for ViT-B, while using 8.6M rather than 86.6M parameters.

limitations: Sharing reduces parameter depth but not computational depth; narrow recurrent models are much weaker; classification and transfer only.
survey_notes: Cleanest iso-FLOP vision recognition result: full sharing is near-lossless only at sufficient width; extra recurrence (12->18) does not buy accuracy in recognition, unlike reasoning tasks (LoopViT, TRM). Contrasts with language results where depth/loops give reasoning gains; recognition is a 'capacity' task. Width-dependence is a design rule the survey should state (also consistent with SPIN 2207.10237 in sibling group). No loop extrapolation tested.

title: RecycleNet: Latent Feature Recycling Leads to Iterative Decision Refinement
relevance_reason: Whole U-Net body is re-applied (weight-tied) for N cycles with late features added back to early layers; randomized cycle count, last-cycle gradients, extrapolation beyond training cycles.
one_sentence: RecycleNet feeds normalized late U-Net decoder features back into early encoder features and re-runs the network for N cycles (randomized up to 3 in training with a warm-up curriculum, last-cycle gradients only); at 7 test cycles it improves nnU-Net Dice on several 3D medical segmentation benchmarks.
key_contributions: Latent feature recycling: input projection I, recycling module R (most of the U-Net), output projection O; recycled features added after normalization.
Robust training schedule: 1 cycle warm-up, then cycle range grows to Nmax=3; gradients only through the last cycle (no BPTT memory cost).
Prediction convergence: Dice increases monotonically with test-time cycles beyond those seen in training.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: KiTS19, MSD Liver tumor, BTCV, AMOS, CHAOS; nnU-Net pipeline
setup.loops_train: Nc ~ U{1..Nmax}, Nmax grows to 3 by curriculum
setup.baselines: nnU-Net, DRU (recurrent U-Net)
setup.benchmarks: Dice on 5-fold CV and public test leaderboards

claims.claim: Recycling improves over nnU-Net and DRU on all datasets except liver tumor (CV), with no added parameters but more compute.
claims.evidence_quote: We show clear performance improvements compared to both baselines across all evaluation datasets but the liver tumor segmentation dataset, where the DRU [18] shows the best cross validation score.

claims.claim: Test-time cycles beyond training (up to 7 vs 3) monotonically increase Dice and saturate ('prediction convergence').
claims.evidence_quote: We observe a monotonous performance increase when increasing the number of recycling cycles during inference, asymptotically converging towards a saturation DSC value.

numbers.what: KiTS CV/Test Dice nnU-Net vs RecycleNet
numbers.quote: Model nnU-Net DRU [18] RecycleNet KiTS CV Test 89.29 89.04 89.58 90.26 89.11

limitations: Higher training memory and training/inference time; small absolute gains in a saturated domain; fixed schedule not tuned per dataset.
builds_on: DRU recurrent U-Net (Wang, Yu et al.)
survey_notes: Early (2023) vision instance of the now-standard looped-LM recipe: randomized loop count, truncated/last-step gradient, and test-time extrapolation with monotone convergence. Lineage to AlphaFold2 recycling. Agrees with LoopMDM/Huginn-style extrapolation; contrasts with DéjàView and ELT where vanilla loops do not extrapolate. Gains are small (<1 Dice point).

title: Universal Speech Transformer
relevance_reason: Applies a Universal Transformer (shared-layer recurrent depth with dynamic depth) to ASR encoder/decoder.
one_sentence: Adapts the Universal Transformer to speech recognition by removing per-step depth embeddings, adding positional embeddings once at the encoder front-end, and using full (not partial ACT-style) hidden updates; reports 3.88-13.7% gains over a speech transformer baseline (abstract only).
key_contributions: First use of universal transformer for ASR (per abstract).
Removes repeated depth/positional embeddings that dilute acoustic information.
Full update of hidden vectors instead of partial update for very deep models.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: LibriSpeech, Switchboard, AISHELL-1
setup.loops_train: dynamic numbers of encoder/decoder layers
setup.baselines: speech transformer

claims.claim: Removing depth embeddings and adding positional embedding only once improves the UT for acoustic inputs.
claims.evidence_quote: we modify its processing framework by removing the depth embedding and only adding the positional embedding once at transformer encoder frontend.

claims.claim: The model outperforms the baseline by 3.88-13.7% on three ASR datasets.
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments on LibriSpeech, Switchboard and AISHELL-1 datasets show that our model outperforms a baseline by 3.88%-13.7%, and surpasses other model with less computation cost.

survey_notes: Abstract only (no fulltext). Early speech evidence that the UT step/depth embedding design does not transfer naively to acoustic inputs: it removes the depth embedding, contrary to language/vision designs that keep step embeddings (LoopViT, DéjàView time conditioning).

title: LAST: Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer
relevance_reason: Six shared AST blocks applied R times; after a full first pass only the class token is looped over cached audio keys/values.
one_sentence: LAST runs 6 shared blocks once over all spectrogram tokens, then loops them R-1 more times updating only the class token with cached audio KV; at R=10 it beats a 12-layer AST on AudioSet (0.3450 vs 0.3379 mAP) with 49.4% fewer parameters and 42% fewer MACs, while full-token looping degrades.
key_contributions: Class-token-only recurrence over fixed, cached audio features: extra passes cost O(D(C^2+NC)) instead of O(D(NC^2+N^2C)), so effective depth grows at near-constant cost.
Controlled comparison under one recipe: sequential AST D in {3,6,9,12} vs full-token loop and LAST with D=6, R in {2..10}.
Robustness to temporal masking and waveform corruptions, and better frozen-feature transfer on audio classification tasks.

setup.model_sizes: D=6 shared blocks, width 768 (49.4% fewer parameters than the 86.1M D=12 baseline); sequential AST 22.3M-86.1M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: AudioSet 1,908,644 clips, 12 epochs from scratch, one seed
setup.loops_train: fixed R in {2,4,6,8,10}, separate model per R
setup.baselines: sequential AST D=3,6,9,12; full-token recurrence with same blocks
setup.benchmarks: AudioSet mAP, throughput, temporal masking, 38 waveform corruptions, 8 frozen-feature transfer tasks (ESC-50, VGGSound, etc.)

claims.claim: At R=10, LAST beats a deeper 12-layer sequential AST on AudioSet with fewer parameters, MACs and higher throughput.
claims.regime: iso_data; looped model has fewer params and fewer FLOPs than deeper baseline
claims.evidence_quote: at 𝑅 = 10, LAST reaches 0.3450 mAP against 0.3379 for sequential 𝐷 = 12 — a 2.1% relative improvement — with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer MACs, and 9.8% higher measured throughput.

claims.claim: Against the parameter-matched 6-layer sequential AST, LAST wins once R >= 6, and the 8 extra passes add only 1.2% compute.
claims.evidence_quote: Against the parameter-matched sequential 𝐷 = 6 baseline, LAST wins once 𝑅 ≥ 6, and its mAP rises at every tested pass count, from 0.3275 at 𝑅 = 2 to 0.3450 at 𝑅 = 10.

claims.claim: Naive full-token recurrence with the same blocks gets worse with more passes despite 5x compute.
claims.evidence_quote: With the same six shared blocks, full-token recurrence falls from 0.3247 mAP at 𝑅 = 2 to 0.3099 at 𝑅 = 10, despite a fivefold increase in computation.

numbers.what: sequential AST D=3 vs D=12 mAP, params, GMACs
numbers.quote: Increasing sequential depth from 𝐷 = 3 to 𝐷 = 12 raises mAP from 0.3049 to 0.3379, at the cost of growing parameters from 22.3M to 86.1M and computation from 12.1 to 48.4 GMACs.

limitations: Single seed; one dataset for training; separately trained model per R (no single-model loop sweep).
survey_notes: Important audio result: full-token looping of an AST hurts with more passes (iso-param), whereas looping only a summary token over cached KV helps cheaply. This is a component-level / KV-shared design akin to cached-KV loop schemes in LMs, and a counterexample to the general claim that more loops help in perception. Fits 'what transfers': loop the integration step, not feature extraction. Compare bViT 2605.10661 (more recurrence does not help recognition at narrow width).

title: Looping Back to Move Forward: Recursive Transformers for Efficient and Flexible Large Multimodal Models
relevance_reason: Whole-stack recursion (R=2) of a 28-layer omni-modal LMM with a modality-specific recursive connector and a per-step monotonic recursion loss.
one_sentence: RecursiveVLM loops the full Ming-Lite-Omni LMM twice, feeding back RMSNormed, MLP-projected, modality-specific fusions of layers 7/14/21/28, and adds a loss enforcing non-decreasing per-token loss across steps; vanilla recursion is worse than no recursion, while this design gains about +3%.
key_contributions: Diagnoses why vanilla recursion fails in LMMs: hidden-state norm growth and low CKA between deep features and input embeddings, with different vision vs text token statistics.
Recursive Connector: RMSNorm + residual MLP back to input-embedding space, modality-specific projections, multi-layer feature fusion.
Monotonic Recursion Loss supervising each step and penalizing loss increases between adjacent steps, giving usable outputs at r=1 and gains at r=2.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: continued pretraining on 6M multimodal + 3M text samples; SFT on 9M+3M general (Data1) or 8M CoT + 2.6M NLP (Data2)
setup.loops_train: R=2 (ablation R=3)
setup.baselines: same model without recursion (R=1) under identical protocol; vanilla recursion; vanilla recursion + RMSNorm
setup.benchmarks: AI2D, MMStar, MMVet, MMMU, MMB, MathVista, OCRBench, HallusionBench

claims.claim: Naive recursion (feeding final hidden states back) is worse than the non-recursive baseline at both steps; RMSNorm alone does not fix it.
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 1, our non-recursive baseline consistently outperforms the vanilla recursive methods at both recursion steps with r = 1 and r = 2.

claims.claim: With the connector and monotonic loss, recursion-trained models beat the non-recursive baseline by 1-2% at r=1 and about +3% at r=2.
claims.evidence_quote: At the second recursion step, performance improves by +3% compared with the non-recursive baseline, confirming monotonic gains and validating our design for deploymentadaptive inference.

claims.claim: R=3 gives diminishing or negative returns on general benchmarks but keeps improving HallusionBench.
claims.evidence_quote: However, a striking trend emerges on the HallusionBench: performance consistently improves with deeper recursion (37.56 → 38.69 → 45.12).

numbers.what: standard (non-recursive) Transformer average over 8 benchmarks (Data1)

limitations: Only R=2-3 studied; gains on general tasks saturate at R=2; recursion doubles inference compute at r=2.
survey_notes: Multimodal retrofit result: vanilla whole-stack recursion of a pretrained LMM hurts (iso-param), and needs a learned connector mapping deep states back to input space plus per-step monotonic supervision. Agrees with language retrofit findings that naive loop retrofits need adaptation/healing (e.g., retrofitted recurrence), and with LoopVAE/ELT that intermediate steps need explicit training. HallusionBench gain with depth is a notable modality-specific benefit. Compute is not matched at r=2.

title: ReLoop-UME: Recurrent Depth with Learnable Retrieval Registers for Universal Multimodal Embedding
relevance_reason: Retrofits Qwen-VL embedding models with a looped middle-to-late block (layers 17-26, T=4) plus persistent register tokens; recurrent depth replaces token-level reasoning for retrieval.
one_sentence: Locates the retrieval-forming layer interval by layer-wise positive/negative separation, loops it T=4 times with five learnable retrieval registers as a fixed workspace, and beats single-pass and reasoning-token UME models on MMEB-V2 at 1.3x the latency of single-pass encoding.
key_contributions: Layer-wise retrieval-discriminability analysis: prefix understanding, retrieval formation (middle-to-late), embedding mapping stages, consistent across Qwen-VL backbones.
Prefix-once / loop retrieval-forming block / suffix-once architecture with Learnable Retrieval Registers that persist across loops and serve as the embedding readout.
Depth-axis alternative to explicit or latent token reasoning in embeddings: 44.9x faster than UME-R1, 1.5x faster than PLUME.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 24 MMEB-V2 training datasets, 5,000 steps, batch 256, InfoNCE
setup.loops_train: T=4 (ablation T=1,2,4,8)
setup.baselines: single-forward version (T=1, M=0) under same recipe; VLM2Vec(-V2), GME, LamRA, DUME, BToks, UME-R1, PLUME
setup.benchmarks: MMEB-V2 (image, video, visual document), MRMR zero-shot

claims.claim: Under the same recipe, looping layers 17-26 with registers improves MMEB-V2 All over the single-forward model by 2.2-2.6 points across three 2B backbones.
claims.evidence_quote: Single forward uses T = 1 and M = 0. The gains support the recipe beyond Qwen2-VL.

claims.claim: Loop placement matters more than compute: full-decoder recurrence uses nearly twice the decoder applications yet performs worse than looping layers 17-26.
claims.regime: iso_param ablation (not FLOP matched; looped mid block uses less compute)
claims.evidence_quote: More computation alone is insufficient: full-decoder recurrence requires 112 decoder applications, nearly twice the 58 of layers 17–26, yet performs worse

claims.claim: Gains saturate at moderate depth: T=4 is best, T=8 slightly worse.
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing T from 1 to 2 improves All from 60.6 to 62.1, and T = 4 reaches 63.2; extending to T = 8 slightly drops to 62.8 despite substantially more decoder applications.

claims.claim: Recurrent depth gives large latency advantages over token-expanded reasoning embedders.
claims.evidence_quote: It reduces per-sample latency from 9023 ms for UME-R1 to 201 ms, corresponding to a 44.9× speedup, and is 1.5× faster than PLUME.

numbers.what: MMEB-V2 All, 2B and 7B
numbers.quote: At approximately 7B parameters, it reaches 65.9 All, surpassing UME-R1 by 1.4 points (65.9 vs. 64.5)

title: Tab-TRM: Tiny Recursive Model for Insurance Pricing on Tabular Data
relevance_reason: TRM-style recursive refinement (shared tiny networks updating a reasoning token and answer token over inner and outer loops) applied to tabular insurance frequency modeling.
one_sentence: Tab-TRM adapts TRM to insurance pricing: feature tokens plus learned answer and reasoning tokens are refined by two tiny shared FNNs over m inner and T outer steps, with full backprop (no ACT); on French MTPL it reaches Poisson deviance competitive with the best neural tabular models at ~15K parameters.
key_contributions: TRM latent recursion for tabular actuarial regression: answer token a and reasoning state z, inner loop on z and outer loop on a, parameters shared across all iterations.
Simplifications vs TRM: no ACT halting and full gradient through the unrolled computation (T*m about 16-64 steps); linearized variant connects to iterative GLM fitting/minimum-bias calibration.
Benchmark on French MTPL against GLM, GAM, FNNs, CAFFT, Credibility Transformer, Tree-like PIN.

setup.loops_train: fixed m inner and T outer steps chosen by Optuna (e.g., m=6, T=3)
setup.baselines: Poisson GLM/GAM, plain FNN, CAFFT, Credibility Transformer, Tree-like PIN (benchmark numbers taken from prior papers)

claims.claim: Tab-TRM's out-of-sample Poisson deviance is competitive with the best neural architectures on French MTPL; baselines are taken from prior publications (unmatched).
claims.evidence_quote: Tab-TRM achieves an out-of-sample Poisson deviance loss of 23.630 × 10−2 (single run) and 23.589 × 10−2 (nagging ensemble), which is competitive with the best network architectures in

claims.evidence_quote: For a typical configuration with m = 6 and T = 3, the effective depth is comparable to a 40 to 50 layer FNN, but with far fewer parameters and a much stronger inductive bias

limitations: Single dataset; no ablation isolating recursion vs a same-size non-recursive model in the main comparison; baselines from literature.

Evidence is weak (unmatched literature baselines, single dataset). Pair with LoopICL 2609.36108 (tabular ICL) as the 'tabular' row: both argue tabular prediction is an iterative-refinement task suited to looping.

title: CoReLoop: Parameter-Efficient Controlled Recurrent Refinement for Audio Deepfake Detection
relevance_reason: Retrofits recurrence into a frozen 24-layer SSL speech encoder (whole encoder re-run) with loop-specific LoRA, input bridge, update gate, anchor memory, and a halting head.
one_sentence: CoReLoop re-runs a frozen W2V-BERT deepfake detector's encoder with loop-specific LoRA, a LoopBridge mapping outputs back to input space, a gated state update and an anchor bank; two passes cut pooled EER from 4.85% to 3.74% with 10M trainable of 598M parameters, while naive output recycling collapses.
key_contributions: Diagnostic: naively feeding the encoder output back as input raises pooled EER from 4.85% to 10.52% and 64.68% over the next passes.
Controlled recurrence on a frozen detector: LoopBridge (input adaptation anchored to prelude features), loop-specific LoRA, UpdateGate, AnchorBank/Reader, ExitBridge; first pass unchanged.
Halting head trained from per-depth losses gives adaptive depth (avg 1.18 passes) at the same EER as fixed two passes.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: official training splits of 14 public speech anti-spoofing datasets; loop modules trained 10 epochs
setup.baselines: frozen detector (T=1), single-pass LoRA with same adapter placement and schedule, naive recurrence controls
setup.benchmarks: Speech DF Arena 14 cross-domain test sets, pooled and macro EER, RTF

claims.claim: Naive recurrence of a frozen single-pass encoder degrades detection sharply, so recurrence must be converted with input adaptation and state control.
claims.evidence_quote: simply feeding this output back without adaptation raises pooled EER from 4.85% at the first pass to 10.52% and 64.68% at the next two.

claims.claim: Two controlled passes reduce pooled EER 4.85% -> 3.74% and beat single-pass LoRA with the same adapters and schedule (4.24%), so adapters alone do not explain the gain.
claims.regime: iso_data; vs LoRA single pass: same trainable params, 2x encoder compute
claims.evidence_quote: It also outperforms single-pass LoRA (4.24% pooled EER), indicating that LoRA adaptation alone does not account for the full gain.

claims.claim: A third pass gives only marginal pooled gains and slightly worse macro EER; adaptive halting matches two passes at 1.18 average passes.
claims.evidence_quote: Adaptive inference achieves 3.73% pooled EER at an average of 1.18 passes, using 41% fewer encoder-core evaluations than fixed two-pass inference.

numbers.what: pooled EER frozen vs CoReLoop T=2
numbers.quote: Table 1 shows that CoReLoop at T = 2 reduces pooled EER from 4.85% to 3.74%, a 22.9% relative reduction over the frozen baseline, with improvements on 10 of the 14 test sets.

numbers.what: 3-seed pooled EER fixed T=2 / T=3 / halting
numbers.quote: fixed T=2, fixed T=3, and adaptive halting obtain pooled EERs of 3.81±0.07%, 3.78±0.08%, and 3.79±0.06% (mean±std), respectively

limitations: Diminishing returns beyond two passes; refinement can regress predictions in some domains; Tmax=3.
survey_notes: Speech-retrofit evidence paralleling RecursiveVLM 2602.09080: naive whole-stack recycling of a pretrained single-pass model collapses (EER 4.85 -> 64.68%), and retrofits need an input-space bridge, gating and per-loop adapters (relaxed sharing). Gains are generalization to unseen attacks, not parameter savings. Loop-LoRA vs single-pass-LoRA control is a good matched comparison (same trainable params).

title: RecRec: Latent Interests Recursive Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
relevance_reason: TRM-style shared-weight recursive reasoner (dual state, deep supervision, 1-step BPTT) refining latent interest vectors on top of a sequential recommender backbone.
one_sentence: RecRec compresses SASRec/BERT4Rec hidden states into a few latent interests and refines them with a TRM-style shared reasoner (separate reasoning state, deep supervision with detached rounds, 1-step BPTT); it beats reasoning-enhanced recommenders and keeps improving past its training depth on 3 of 4 datasets.
key_contributions: Decouples sequence space, reasoning state S and multi-vector prediction state M (latent interests), unlike ReaRec/LARES which reason in the backbone's single d-dim state.
Context Compressor with interest-diversity regularizer plus a Recursive Reasoner trained by deep supervision (K rounds x T steps, detached between rounds), RL-free two-stage training.
Inference-depth sweep 0-16: largest gain from the first pass; small further gains beyond training depth N=9 on three datasets.

setup.loops_train: K x T = 9 reasoning steps with deep supervision
setup.baselines: SASRec, BERT4Rec, ReaRec, LARES (depth-recurrent) and other reasoning-enhanced recommenders

claims.claim: At training depth N=9, RecRec beats the best reasoning-enhanced baseline in NDCG@10 by 4.3-14.8% across four datasets.
claims.evidence_quote: RecRec (S) improves NDCG@10 over the best reasoning-enhanced baseline by 14.8% on Steam, 9.3% on MicroLens, 8.2% on V-Shop, and 4.3% on S-Shop.

claims.claim: Deep supervision with detached rounds lets inference depth extend past the training depth with small gains on 3 of 4 datasets (MicroLens saturates near 4 and declines).
claims.evidence_quote: on three of four datasets, performance is sustained past the training-time depth 𝑁 = 9 with small additional gains.

numbers.what: NDCG@20 jump from N=0 to N=1 on S-Shop and Steam (SASRec)
numbers.quote: for example from 0.0966 to 0.103 on S-Shop (SASRec) and from 0.0496 to 0.058 on Steam (SASRec).

limitations: Extrapolation gains are small and not universal (MicroLens declines beyond N~4).
survey_notes: Recommendation row: TRM recipe (dual state, deep supervision, 1-step gradient) transfers and supports modest depth extrapolation. Modality tag 'graph' used for user-item interaction data (no recsys tag in schema).

key_contributions: Generative Equilibrium Transformer: injection transformer plus weight-tied equilibrium transformer solving for a fixed point, with near parameter-free class conditioning.
Fully offline one-step diffusion distillation from noise/image pairs; parity with online distillation on a 1M-sample data budget.

Preliminary scaling study for implicit models: GET matches much larger explicit ViTs; more test-time fixed-point iterations improve FID; a compute-optimal 'sweet spot' model size at fixed training FLOPs.

title: Deeply-Recursive Convolutional Network for Image Super-Resolution
relevance_reason: Pre-transformer weight-tied recursive conv layer (up to 16 recursions) for super-resolution with per-recursion supervision; lineage for looped vision models.
one_sentence: DRCN applies one shared conv layer up to 16 times for single-image super-resolution, supervising every recursion through a shared reconstruction net and adding an input-to-output skip; more recursions raise PSNR at fixed parameters and the ensemble of all recursions beats any single depth.
key_contributions: Very deep recursion (16) of a single conv layer to enlarge receptive field without new parameters.
Recursive supervision: every intermediate recursion is decoded and supervised, then predictions are ensembled.
Skip connection from input to reconstruction to preserve the low-resolution signal across recursions.

setup.loops_train: fixed recursion depth (1, 6, 11, 16 studied; 16 default)
setup.baselines: A+, SRCNN, RFL, SelfEx

claims.evidence_quote: We trained four models with different numbers of recursions: 1, 6, 11, and 16. Four models use the same number of parameters except the weights used for ensemble.

claims.claim: No single recursion depth is best across scales; ensembling intermediate recursions significantly helps.
claims.evidence_quote: There is no single recursion depth that works the best across all scale factors. Ensemble of intermediate predictions significantly improves performance.

title: Learning When to Recur: Token-Adaptive Recursion for Imbalanced Ophthalmic Domain Incremental Learning
relevance_reason: Token-adaptive recursion (gated early exit, up to Kmax=3) over LoRA-adapted final blocks of a frozen ophthalmic foundation model, within a continual-learning framework.

claims.evidence_quote: Looking at the results with 1 block, more iterations lead to significantly higher SI-SDR performance without increasing the trainable parameters of the overall model: 10.2 → 13.6 dB and 7.1 → 12.3 dB for separation and denoising, respectively.
